questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has 3 months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation, with a resting heart rate of 56. In the examination you tell the examiner you will look for the reflex sign of hypothyroidism. Which technique best shows it?
options: Knee jerk with Jendrassik reinforcement, looking for a brisk, wide-amplitude response
Plantar response with a blunt stimulus, looking for an upgoing great toe
Ankle jerk with her kneeling on a chair, watching for a slow relaxation phase
Biceps jerk with her arm relaxed, looking for spread to finger flexion
questions.why: Hypothyroidism slows the relaxation phase of the reflex (it is 'hung up'), not the contraction. The ankle jerk with the patient kneeling on a chair, feet hanging free, shows this best.
notes: Brisk, wide-amplitude reflexes suggest hyperthyroidism or an upper motor neurone lesion, and reinforcement only helps when a reflex is hard to get.
An upgoing plantar is an upper motor neurone sign and plays no part in hypothyroidism.
Spread of a reflex to nearby muscles is an upper motor neurone sign; it does not show the delayed relaxation seen in hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, of average build with no heart disease, has TSH 52 mIU/L, free T4 4.3 pmol/L and strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies. Her sodium and potassium are normal, and she has no pigmentation, postural drop or hypos. Which treatment plan is best?
options: Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily before breakfast; recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks
Levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily, increasing by 25 micrograms monthly on free T4 alone
Liothyronine 20 micrograms twice daily; recheck free T3 and TSH in 2 weeks
Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily with breakfast; recheck TSH in 2 weeks
questions.why: A young patient without heart disease can start the full replacement dose of levothyroxine, about 1.6 micrograms/kg (around 100 micrograms), on an empty stomach. TSH takes about 6 weeks to settle, so check it 6 to 8 weeks after each dose change.
notes: Starting low and titrating slowly is for older patients or those with ischaemic heart disease; here it just delays recovery, and TSH, not free T4 alone, guides the dose.
Liothyronine is not first-line replacement: its short half-life gives swings in T3, and levothyroxine is the standard treatment.
Food reduces levothyroxine absorption, and TSH has not reached steady state at 2 weeks, so the result would mislead dosing.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has Hashimoto thyroiditis and an anaemia with Hb 104 g/L and MCV 118 fL. Her B12 and folate results are pending. A colleague suggests starting folic acid now to save time. Why is giving folic acid alone risky if she turns out to be B12 deficient?
options: It corrects the anaemia while B12-dependent nerve damage keeps progressing
It competes with B12 for uptake in the terminal ileum, worsening the deficiency
It drives such rapid red cell production that it causes severe hypokalaemia
It stimulates parietal cell autoantibodies and speeds up the atrophic gastritis
questions.why: Folate can bypass the methylfolate trap and restore DNA synthesis, so the blood count improves. It cannot replace B12's role with methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in making myelin, so subacute combined degeneration progresses without being noticed.
notes: Folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel by a different mechanism, and it does not block uptake of the B12-intrinsic factor complex.
Hypokalaemia can occur when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated, but it is not why folate alone is avoided. The worry is irreversible nerve damage.
Folic acid has no effect on the autoimmune process in pernicious anaemia.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto thyroiditis and a macrocytic anaemia (MCV 118 fL). Pernicious anaemia is suspected. In this condition, autoimmune gastritis destroys the cells that make intrinsic factor. Which part of the gut is mainly affected?
options: Gastric antrum, where the gastrin-secreting G cells lie
Proximal duodenum, where B12 is transferred onto intrinsic factor
Terminal ileum, where the B12-intrinsic factor complex is absorbed
Gastric body and fundus, where the parietal cells lie
questions.why: Parietal cells, which secrete acid and intrinsic factor, sit in the oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body and fundus. Autoimmune gastritis attacks this area and spares the antrum, so gastrin rises as acid output falls.
notes: The antrum is typically spared in autoimmune gastritis. Its G cells overproduce gastrin in response to the low acid.
B12 does bind intrinsic factor in the duodenum, but the intrinsic factor is made in the stomach. The duodenum is not the autoimmune target.
The terminal ileum is where B12 is absorbed, and it is affected in Crohn disease or resection. It is not the site of the lesion in pernicious anaemia.
